title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam, not a failure of a deployed AI product. Scammers used AI tools to generate personalized, convincing emails that impersonated a named public figure, Terry Gross, in order to extract payment from recipients. The AI capability at work is text generation that pulls from publicly available information about a target, producing messages detailed enough to seem credible at first contact.

The failure point is not inside an AI company's deployment but in the hands of bad actors using general-purpose AI to scale and personalize fraud. What made the scam harder to detect was that the messages referenced specific details of recipients' work, removing the generic quality that has historically made phishing emails easier to spot. The tell, noticed by at least one recipient, was a procedural irregularity, contact coming directly from the named host rather than through production staff, rather than anything in the text itself.

What is not established is who is behind the scam, what specific AI tools were used, whether any payments were successfully collected, or whether any investigation has produced findings or charges.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
Scammers have been sending personalized emails impersonating Terry Gross, host of the NPR program Fresh Air, to solicit fees from potential interview guests. Authors, entertainers and other public figures have received highly detailed messages that reference their work and appear professional, making them seem legitimate. The emails eventually request payment, typically around $250, for supposed production costs. Misericordia University history professor Jennifer Black initially felt excited about the invitation but grew suspicious when the email came directly from Gross herself rather than a producer, and when artificial intelligence seemed evident in the messaging.

WHYY, NPR and Fresh Air have confirmed awareness of the fraudulent emails and are working with law enforcement to investigate. The scam has also targeted other celebrities including comedians Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler and journalist Katie Couric. WHYY stated it never charges guests for interviews and that any communication requesting payment should be considered fraudulent. Cybersecurity experts advise people to verify requests through official contact information and to be skeptical of any requests for money or personal credentials, as artificial intelligence now enables convincingly personalized scams that target specific individuals based on their public profiles.
